PurposeTo develop and validate a fully automated pipeline that measures skeletal muscle and adipose tissue at L1 and L3 on routine CT with varied scan ranges, slice orders and contrast phases, rejects levels outside the scan and converts measures to non-contrast equivalents.

Materials and methodsThe pipeline (sarco) combines orientation detection, L1/L3 localisation with out-of-range rejection, U-Net segmentation, six-class contrast-phase estimation, phase-specific conversion to non-contrast-equivalent values and, as an auxiliary output, muscle and marrow age estimation. We evaluated it on five single-centre datasets (4986 series): agreement with radiologist-corrected labels using five-fold cross-fitting (2025 series), artificially truncated scans, contrast-enhanced series paired with non-contrast series of the same examination, and the prognostic value of fully automated measures in 2006 patients after curative cancer surgery. TotalSegmentator served as a comparator.

ResultsOn held-out folds, L3 skeletal muscle area (SMA) agreed with the reference (intraclass correlation coefficient 0.983; bias +1.35 cm{superscript 2}). On truncated scans processed with cross-fitted localisation models, the chosen L3 slice was off by half a vertebra or more in 4.7-5.6% of volumes (TotalSegmentator 11.3-14.3%). Four-group phase accuracy was 0.949, exceeding TotalSegmentator in scans shorter than 400 mm (0.952-0.960 vs 0.643-0.668), and conversion reduced the root mean square error of L3 muscle attenuation against the same-examination non-contrast series from 7.96 to 2.81 HU. Combined age estimates had a mean absolute error of 6.5 years. Automatically measured low muscle mass increased the cross-validated Unos C of the baseline model by 0.034 (95% CI 0.009-0.053; cancer-specific survival) and 0.031 (0.016-0.048; overall survival), whereas converted L3 muscle attenuation added 0.012 (-0.005 to 0.024) for overall survival.

ConclusionThe pipeline provides robust, contrast-phase-aware body composition measures from routine CT with varied scan ranges and reproduces known prognostic associations without manual input.

Short abstractWe validated a fully automated pipeline for L1/L3 body composition on routine CT. It handled truncated scans, estimated the contrast phase, converted measures to non-contrast equivalents, agreed closely with radiologist-corrected labels and reproduced prognostic associations in 2006 surgical patients.

title: Segment Anything for Microscopy 2
abstract: Foundation models have advanced microscopy image segmentation, but existing models are trained on two-dimensional data, struggle with complex structures in volumetric data, and address only a narrow range of analysis tasks. Here we present Segment Anything for Microscopy 2 (μSAM2), a foundation model that adapts SAM2 to joint 2D and 3D segmentation in light and electron microscopy. Trained on annotations of more than 23 million cells and nuclei and 1.6 million cellular structures, μSAM2 achieves state-of-the-art automatic and interactive segmentation and outperforms generalist and specialist methods on volumetric data. Dedicated models further enable accurate mitochondrion and nucleus segmentation in electron microscopy. Beyond segmentation, μSAM2 supports pixel and object classification from few annotations as well as cell tracking in 2D and 3D time-lapse data. All functionality is available in the user-friendly μSAM napari plugin. We demonstrated the capabilities of μSAM2 on challenging use cases spanning developmental biology, organoid research, cardiac physiology, and histopathology.

title: Restoring Marčenko-Pastur noise estimation and denoising of diffusion MRI under common image reconstruction
abstract: Diffusion magnetic resonance imaging can reveal microstructure in the living brain, but the measurements are inherently noisy. Marčenko–Pastur denoising is a widely used remedy, helping to separate signal from noise under a simplified noise covariance model. However, we find that the model breaks under common image reconstructions across 28 public in vivo datasets, resulting in weaker denoising than intended. We restore the intended denoising behavior with a noise covariance model estimated from the reconstructed images, and validate the estimated model on repeated ex vivo and in vivo scans. The method requires no additional measurements or knowledge of the reconstruction, opening headroom for microstructure analyses in both existing and newly acquired data.

title: Cortical surface area is an independent predictor of incident dementia
abstract: Cortical surface area (cSA) is associated with intelligence and cognition, yet structural MRI studies of neurodegeneration in Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias (ADRD) have emphasized quantification of cortical thickness (cTH) and volume, with very limited evaluation of cSA. We examined whether cSA of AD-relevant brain regions provide diagnostic, prognostic, and biological information beyond cTH and volume across 5,430 participants (3,124 cognitively unimpaired; 1,634 mild cognitive impairment [MCI]; 672 ADRD) from three aging and dementia cohorts: the National Alzheimer’s Coordinating Center, Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, and Carotids and Minds study. In cross-sectional analyses, cSA and cTH showed weak correlation, and lower cSA was independently associated with greater odds of MCI and ADRD after adjustment for cTH and covariates. Participants with both low cSA and low cTH had greater risk of MCI and ADRD compared to low cSA, cTH, or volume alone. In longitudinal models, baseline cSA predicted incident ADRD independent from cTH, and combined cSA/cTH models outperformed cSA, cTH, or volume alone for predicting incident ADRD over a mean follow-up of 4.3 years. Complementing these findings, proteomics analyses revealed distinct signatures associated with cSA compared to cTH. Overall, these findings support cSA as a clinically informative and biologically distinct dimension of AD-related cortical vulnerability.

title: MeXalign – A Segmentation Mask-Based Registration Pipeline for Multimodal Single-Cell Analysis
abstract: Leveraging the power of multimodal imaging relies on accurate coregistration of yet fundamentally different modalities. Reliable cell-to-cell correspondence is especially challenging as consecutive tissue sections do not necessarily contain identical cells or cellular structures. Here we present MeXalign, a segmentation-mask-based coregistration pipeline designed to integrate multimodal images acquired sequentially from the same specimen at single-cell resolution. Single-cell segmentation masks provide a modality-independent representation of cellular morphology and spatial organization. MeXalign was tested based on the two platforms, laser ablation inductively coupled plasma time-of-flight mass spectrometry (LA-ICP-TOFMS) and immunofluorescence (IF) microscopy. As a prerequisite, each modality integrates membrane and/or nucleus labels for accurate segmentation. The added value of MeXalign was highlighted for imaging of cell models deposited on glass slides and tissue sections. The performance of coregistration was validated on cytospins, murine tumor and human skin samples. A dedicated scoring system was introduced allowing to assess the quality of image coregistration. The robustness towards under-segmentation and downstream image analysis was evaluated on LA-ICP-TOFMS with and without coregistration, investigating metal drug uptake, barcoding and cellular phenotyping. A showcase study on cancer cells exposed to nanoparticles proved the accuracy, as the nanoparticle distribution was preserved at a subcellular level when using MeXalign. While all examples show the overall improved quality of segmentation, other benefits of complementary labelings can be anticipated, especially for cellular features unique to one modality. title: Discovery of latent clinical phenotypes through optimal transport of brain dynamics
abstract: The increasing availability of large clinical neuroimaging datasets has enabled the discovery of objective, data-driven clinical phenotypes. However, current approaches typically rely on structural or static functional metrics, thereby overlooking the rich information embedded in brain dynamics. To address this limitation, we developed a computational framework combining a Gaussian Hidden Markov Model (HMM) with Optimal Transport (OT) theory. By representing individual brain dynamics within a shared latent state space, our approach quantifies how much one subject's state-transition dynamics would need to be modified to match another subject's state occupancy distribution, providing a pairwise measure of inter-individual variability that captures temporal aspects of brain function. We applied this framework to multiple sclerosis (MS), a condition where substantial within-group heterogeneity challenges traditional clinical classification. Analyzing resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging data from 122 patients with relapsing-remitting MS and 97 matched healthy controls, the HMM identified three latent states with distinct connectivity patterns. While patients showed an altered temporal organization of recurrent brain states relative to healthy controls, reflected in selective differences in state occupancy and dwell time, we focused on quantifying heterogeneity specifically within the MS cohort. Clustering patients according to OT-based dissimilarities revealed two subgroups with distinct clinical disability and structural disease burden. Crucially, this stratification was not detectable when applying clustering procedures to static functional connectivity, supporting the added value of dynamical features. Our results establish a general methodological framework for extracting clinically relevant phenotypes from temporal brain dynamics, with potential applications across neurological and psychiatric conditions characterized by phenotypic heterogeneity.

title: MR-based normative volumetric analyses reveal genotype-dependent brain anomalies in FGFR -related craniosynostoses
abstract: Craniostenosis, a cranial malformation due to premature suture fusion, includes rare FGFR -related conditions such as Crouzon (CS), Muenke (MS), and Apert (AS) syndromes. These mutations affect skull but also brain development and are associated with variable neurodevelopmental outcomes. This brain impairment is still poorly described and understood, prompting for neuroimaging anatomical studies. We thus investigated regional brain growth and volumetric scaling in patients with these three syndromes and non-syndromic non- FGFR -related craniostenoses, using a normative modelling framework. We analyzed a rare set of brain MRI from 65 patients close to first cranial surgery time (30 CS among which 23 pre-surgery, 4 AS, 6 MS, 23 non-syndromic) and 130 typically developing controls. Millimetric 3D T1-weighted images were segmented into 6 cortical and 3 subcortical regions (AssemblyNet, Morphologist). After harmonization (ComBat), normative growth curves (Turner model) and static scaling curves (power-law model, effect of brain size regardless of age) were derived in controls. Patient deviations were assessed using permutation tests on mean normalized distance to typical model and abnormality rates (10th/90th percentiles). Patients with CS showed typical brain volumes for age except for enlarged ventricles, but slightly overscaled frontal volumes for brain size. Non-syndromic patients showed very similar volume distribution for age and brain size than CS ones. Patients with AS displayed increased total brain, temporal, cerebellar and central volumes for age, with overscaled temporal and cerebellar regions but underscaled frontal volumes for brain size. Patients with MS showed a similar, though milder, pattern: increased temporal volume for age, with temporal overscaling but frontal underscaling for frain size. Our findings reveal genotype-dependent brain anomalies in FGFR -related craniosynostoses, with a convergent pattern of temporal–frontal disproportions in AS and MS, associated with very specific mutations in the FGFR2 and 3 genes respectively, contrasting with a much more typical brain organization in more heterogeneous CS and non-syndromic patients. Beyond the pathophysiological meaning of these results, which call for a larger similar study covering as wide a range of patient variability as possible, our work highlights the relevance of normative modelling approach for characterizing rare craniofacial disorders using clinical MRI datasets.

title: Normative Modeling of Structural and Diffusion MRI for Epilepsy Diagnosis and Classification
abstract: Background: and Objectives: Normative modeling expresses an individual's brain measures as deviations from a large healthy reference and has been advanced as a route to precision imaging biomarkers in epilepsy, where structural abnormality is distributed rather than confined to the presumed focus. Whether this framework can inform clinical classification from clinically acquired T1-weighted and diffusion MRI is untested. We asked whether normative deviations discriminate between (1) epilepsy and functional seizures; (2) focal and generalized epilepsy; and (3) drug-resistant and drug-responsive epilepsy. Methods: We retrospectively studied patients with epilepsy or functional seizures without comorbid epilepsy who underwent 3-Tesla epilepsy-protocol MRI at the University of Pennsylvania. Morphometric deviation scores (cortical thickness, subcortical volume) were derived from CentileBrain (n>37,000 healthy references). White matter fractional anisotropy and mean diffusivity profiles were referenced to harmonized Human Connectome Project cohorts. Lobar composites, hemispheric asymmetry indices, and whole-tract means were compared with rank-sum tests; discrimination was summarized as area under the ROC curve (AUC) with bootstrap confidence intervals and Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Whole-brain deviation burden was examined as a secondary analysis. Minimum detectable effects were estimated by Monte Carlo simulation at 80% power (α=0.05). Results: We included 273 patients with epilepsy (203 focal, 37 generalized, 33 unclassified; 97 drug-resistant, 176 drug-responsive) and 32 with functional seizures. In the primary analyses, no regional or tract-level normative measure distinguished epilepsy from functional seizures, focal from generalized epilepsy, or drug-resistant from drug-responsive epilepsy; AUCs did not exceed 0.62, with upper confidence limits up to 0.72. In the secondary analysis, whole-brain morphometric deviation burden was modestly higher in epilepsy than in functional seizures (AUC 0.66, 95% CI 0.57-0.74) but did not separate the within-epilepsy comparisons. The study could detect AUC ≥0.65 for epilepsy versus functional seizures, ≥0.64 for focal versus generalized, and ≥0.60 for drug-resistant versus drug-responsive epilepsy. Discussion: Univariate normative deviation summaries from clinical MRI do not currently distinguish these groups well enough to guide care. Whole-brain deviation burden, the only summary measure that differed after correction, was detectable at the group level but insufficient for individual-level classification. Progress may require network-targeted analysis of patient-specific deviations and multimodal integration.

title: Integrating Histopathology Foundation Models and PRAME Immunohistochemistry in Melanoma Diagnosis
abstract: Background: The histopathological diagnosis of challenging melanocytic lesions remains limited by substantial interobserver variability. Although computational pathology foundation models demonstrated promising diagnostic performance, their predictions are often difficult to interpret in terms of established criteria. Objective: We evaluated a diagnostic framework combining foundation-model-based whole-slide image analysis, automated prediction of morphological features, and manually assessed PRAME immunohistochemistry. Methods: Using the Virchow2 foundation model and STAMP framework, we analyzed a retrospective cohort of 1,000 melanocytic lesions undergoing PRAME immunohistochemistry. Models were trained on 800 cases and evaluated on a temporally held-out test cohort of 200 cases. Results: The slide-level malignancy classifier achieved a test AUROC of 0.970 (AUPRC 0.984). Separate models predicted established histopathological criteria with high discrimination, including ulceration (AUROC 0.991) and dermal mitoses (AUROC 0.966). In contrast, predicting PRAME expression from H&E images alone showed lower performance (AUROC 0.776-0.780 for PRAME scores 4 and 0). An integrated model combining the slide-level malignancy score, AI-predicted morphological features, and manual PRAME status achieved an AUROC of 0.972 (AUPRC 0.975), comparable to the standalone classifier. In multivariable analysis, PRAME score 4 versus 0 was strongly associated with malignancy (adjusted OR 35.04, 95% CI 17.39-74.62). Conclusions: These findings demonstrate the feasibility of combining foundation-model-based histopathological analysis with established morphological criteria and PRAME immunohistochemistry. Although the integrated framework did not substantially improve overall discrimination, it provides a structured approach for incorporating complementary histopathological and immunohistochemical information into AI-assisted assessment of melanocytic lesions.

title: Deep learning of point-of-care lung ultrasound and clinical data for pulmonary tuberculosis triage in Uganda
abstract: Rationale: Point of care lung ultrasound is portable and radiation free and could extend tuberculosis screening to settings without chest radiography, but no standardized criteria exist for interpreting it for tuberculosis. Objectives: To develop and internally evaluate deep learning models that classify pulmonary tuberculosis from lung ultrasound images, alone and combined with routine clinical variables, and to derive an abbreviated scanning protocol. Methods: In a prospective study in Kampala, Uganda (2023 to 2025), we enrolled people aged 13 years or older with microbiologically confirmed pulmonary tuberculosis, their household contacts, and symptomatic people with other respiratory conditions. One still frame from each of 12 lung ultrasound zones was analyzed with an attention-based multiple-instance learning network. We compared clinical-only (random forest), ultrasound only, and combined models and derived a 6 zone protocol from training set attention weights. Participants were allocated to training (n = 223), validation (n = 20), and held-out test (n = 73) sets. Results: Of 318 enrolled participants, 316 were analyzed (118 with and 198 without tuberculosis). In the test set, areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve were 0.88 (95% confidence interval, 0.80 to 0.95) for the clinical-only model; 0.93 (0.86 to 0.97) and 0.95 (0.89 to 0.99) for the 12 zone ultrasound-only and combined models; and 0.91 (0.83 to 0.97) and 0.93 (0.86 to 0.99) for the corresponding 6-zone models. At 90% sensitivity, specificity was 82.2% (34.9 to 97.8) for the 12-zone combined model and 91.1% (25.0 to 98.0) for the 6-zone combined model. Point estimates for all 12-zone models and the 6-zone combined model met the 2025 World Health Organization minimum accuracy targets for a high-sensitivity screening test (≥90% sensitivity, ≥60% specificity). Conclusion: Lung ultrasound analyzed with attention-based deep learning and combined with clinical variables showed high internal discrimination for pulmonary tuberculosis, and a simplified 6-zone protocol retained most of this performance. External validation in intended-use screening populations is needed

title: Rapid screening of target-specific isotope labeling protocols for in situ NMR of bacterial membrane proteins
abstract: We describe an approach for the efficient development of targeted isotope labeling protocols leading to nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) structural studies of bacterial membrane proteins in intact cells and native outer membrane (OM) vesicles (OMVs). The assay relies on the bioorthogonal non-canonical amino acid tagging (BONCAT) approach for metabolic incorporation of an azide-bearing residue, followed by copper-catalyzed azide-alkyne cycloaddition (CuAAC) to an alkyne-functionalized fluorescent dye. Fluorescence detection in SDS-PAGE provides a rapid way to test samples for off-target background signal from endogenous proteins, bypassing the need for intensive NMR screening experiments. Using this approach, we develop an optimized protocol that enables high-resolution NMR spectra to be obtained in situ with negligible background signal. The BONCAT approach also enables target-specific fluorescence or nano-gold labeling of proteins at the OM surface, further extending the utility of this protocol for correlative structure-activity studies of membrane proteins in situ.

title: Traumatic microbleeds are associated with unfavorable outcome out to 1 year after mild traumatic brain injury: A TRACK-TBI Study
abstract: ABSTRACT Importance Traumatic microbleeds (TMB) are commonly observed in mild TBI (mTBI). However, questions remain regarding their long-term prognostic significance. Objective Determine whether traumatic microbleeds predict unfavorable outcome after mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI) Design The prospective longitudinal observational T ransforming R esearch a nd C linical K nowledge in T raumatic B rain Injury (TRACK-TBI) study enrolled acute TBI patients presenting to Emergency Departments (ED) at 18 U.S. Level 1 trauma centers between 2/26/2014-08/08/2018. CT and MRI were evaluated using the National Institutes of Health-National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NIH-NINDS) TBI Common Data Elements. Outcome was assessed using the Glasgow Outcome Scale–Extended (GOSE-TBI) at 2 weeks and 3, 6, and 12 months post-injury. Setting 18 U.S. Level 1 trauma centers Participants 929 GCS 13-15 patients ≥17 years old (38.5 ± 16.5 years, 66% male) who underwent clinical head CT ≤24 hours and brain MRI at 2 weeks post-injury and had at least one GOSE-TBI outcome score during 1 year follow-up. Exposure(s) Acute non-penetrating head trauma Main Outcome(s) and Measure(s) Frequency and co-occurrence of CT and MR features; incomplete recovery (GOSE-TBI <8 vs. =8) and unfavorable outcome (GOSE-TBI <5 vs. ≥5) at 2 weeks and 3, 6, and 12 months Results Generalized estimating equation models showed that TMBs and/or IVH were strongly associated with unfavorable outcome (GOSE-TBI <5 vs. ≥5) at 3, 6, and 12 months post-injury, but not with incomplete recovery (GOSE-TBI <8 vs. =8). For prediction of GOSE-TBI <5 vs. ≥5, TMBs surpassed the importance of all demographic and baseline clinical predictors throughout the 1-year follow-up period. For prediction of incomplete recovery (GOSE-TBI <8 vs. =8), brain contusions, subarachnoid hemorrhage, and subdural hematoma were more important throughout the 12-month follow-up period. Conclusions and Relevance Traumatic microbleeds (TMB) are common in mTBI. The presence of ≥4 TMBs and/or IVH is strongly associated with unfavorable outcome (GOSE-TBI <5) after mTBI out to at least 1 year, even after controlling for other neuroimaging abnormalities and demographic and clinical predictors. title: Manifestation-Guided Adaptation of CT Foundation Model for Early Neurological Prognosis after ECPR
abstract: PurposeTo develop a data-efficient, clinically guided transfer-learning framework for hyperacute neurological outcome prediction from head CT in patients undergoing extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) after cardiac arrest by leveraging free-text radiology report. MethodsThis retrospective study included 683 patients with available CT examination and radiology reports from December 2015 to November 2025. The primary outcome distinguished favorable neurological outcomes (Cerebral Performance Category [CPC] 1-2) from neurological death due to brain death or cerebral herniation (CPC 5). A cross-attention adaptor jointly learned to predict neurological outcome and five report-derived manifestations of brain injury from a frozen pretrained head CT encoder. Outcome prediction used CT images alone at inference. The manifestation-guided adaptor, trained with and without additional patients who contributed only manifestation labels, was compared with outcome-only adaptor and two pooled-feature baselines. Performance was summarized as mean {+/-} SD across five held-out folds. ResultsOf 683 patients, 197 were eligible for outcome evaluation (63 with favorable outcomes and 134 with neurological death), and 486 formed the manifestation-only cohort. The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) was 0.918 {+/-} 0.044 for the outcome-only adaptor. The manifestation-guided adaptor achieved an AUROC of 0.927 {+/-} 0.042. With additional manifestation-only training data, the adaptor achieved the mean AUROC (0.929 {+/-} 0.037), specificity (93.7% {+/-} 6.5%), with a sensitivity of 79.9% {+/-} 9.2%. ConclusionManifestation-guided adaptation outperforms outcome-only adaptation for neurological outcome prediction from hyperacute head CT after ECPR. Report-derived manifestation labels enabled training with additional examinations without eligible outcome labels while preserving CT-only prediction.

title: Age and sex differences in lateral ventricle choroid plexus volume in a large, manually segmented, multi-site MRI dataset
abstract: Background The choroid plexus, which produces cerebrospinal fluid and forms the blood–cerebrospinal fluid barrier, is of growing interest in psychiatric and neurodegenerative neuroimaging. However, most volumetric studies have relied on automated segmentation tools that agree poorly with manual tracing, and manually segmented samples have been small, single-site, and narrow in age range. Methods We analyzed DataPlex, a dataset of 700 manually segmented lateral ventricle choroid plexus labels from 3T T1-weighted MRI scans (ages 6–90 years) drawn from 29 studies and three scanner manufacturers (35 study-by-manufacturer sites). Generalized least squares models accounting for within-site dependence tested associations of age, sex, scanner manufacturer, image resolution, a registration-based image-quality metric, and intracranial volume with choroid plexus and lateral ventricle volumes, including nonlinear (spline) and sex-interaction terms. Exploratory models tested associations between these volumes and cognitive performance. Results In 699 scans, choroid plexus volume increased linearly with age (63–69 mm³ per decade) and was 56–65 mm³ larger in males than females after covariate adjustment; the age association did not differ by sex. Lateral ventricle volume increased nonlinearly with age, with steeper age-related enlargement in males than females. Scanner manufacturer and image resolution were associated with left lateral ventricle volume; scanner manufacturer was associated with choroid plexus volume only in a sensitivity model. The image-quality metric was not associated with any outcome. In exploratory analyses, larger choroid plexus volume was associated with lower inhibitory control, working memory, and episodic memory scores and with higher emotion recognition scores (uncorrected p < 0.05). Conclusions In the largest and most diverse manually segmented choroid plexus dataset to date, choroid plexus volume differed by age and sex and was less sensitive than lateral ventricle volume to acquisition differences. These estimates provide reference benchmarks for automated segmentation tools and support adjustment for demographic and technical covariates.

title: Disease-specific versus symptom-specific neuroimaging phenotypes across Alzheimer’s Disease, Parkinson’s Disease, and Small Vessel Disease
abstract: Background Neurodegenerative disorders are common in ageing populations, and arise from several distinct pathophysiological causes. Yet, they also share many symptoms, including cognitive and neuropsychiatric ones. It is unclear to what extent the impact of neurodegeneration on brain systems is unique or shared across disorders, and whether shared symptoms are driven by degeneration of the same brain systems. Methods We collected data from n=251 participants with Alzheimer’s Disease, Parkinson’s Disease, Small Vessel Disease, and age-matched healthy controls. All participants underwent harmonized cognitive and neuropsychiatric assessment and were scanned using the UK-Biobank MRI protocol capturing features including brain volume, white matter lesions and microstructure, tract volume, iron content, and functional connectivity. Results We replicated established case-control brain changes in Alzheimer’s Disease, Parkinson’s Disease and Small Vessel Disease compared to healthy controls. Leveraging this joint standardised dataset, we identified distinct neuroimaging features of individual neurodegenerative disorders, providing evidence for robust diagnosis-specific brain changes. Importantly, however, there was also a large degree of transdiagnostic similarity across neuroimaging markers. Testing for transdiagnostic associations between symptoms and brain phenotypes, we found that lower medial frontal pole connectivity to primary motor cortex was preferentially associated with apathy, fatigue, and depression; whereas cingulum microstructure was associated with cognitive deficits across diagnoses. Conclusions These results demonstrate that different neurodegenerative diseases are characterised by dissociable brain changes, but also common transdiagnostic and symptom-associated features. This suggests that shared symptoms across neurodegeneration may in part be driven by overlapping impact on key brain systems, such as changes in medial frontal pole connectivity and cingulum microstructure. Our work highlights that multimodal imaging biomarkers can help understand and parse symptomatic heterogeneity in neurodegenerative and ageing populations.

title: Patient, carer and clinical stakeholder views on using artificial intelligence and machine learning for the histopathological diagnosis of duodenal biopsies
abstract: Objective Biopsies are examined under the microscope by a pathologist, giving a diagnosis, which guides treatment and predicts prognosis. A shortage of pathologists and increasing workload leads to diagnostic delays, while for duodenal (small intestinal) biopsies, variable diagnostic concordance between pathologists limits accuracy. These challenges have motivated us to develop an artificial intelligence (AI)-mediated approach for the automated diagnosis of up to 80% of duodenal biopsies (i.e., most cases of the two most frequent diagnoses: coeliac disease and “normal”). We set out to understand patient, carer and stakeholder views regarding the adoption of such technology. Methods and Analysis We conducted mixed-methods stakeholder engagement (February 2024 to June 2026). We ran a national online patients’ and carers’ questionnaire (n=231 respondents) and four UK focus-group workshops, one of which additionally captured Likert-scale attitudes 1 immediately before and after a structured educational session (n=34 matched pairs). Healthcare professionals completed an online questionnaire (n=37) and took part in a structured workshop. Quantitative data were summarised descriptively; free-text and workshop data were analysed thematically and triangulated across all sources. Results Most patients and carers supported AI-reliant diagnosis (68.4%) and would strongly trust systems with formal regulatory approval (66.7%). Most wanted to be informed if AI was used (73.6%), but only 52.4% felt explicit permission was necessary. Qualitative themes centred on clear and available evidence of accuracy, human oversight, transparent communication and clear terminology, with the term ‘machine learning’ being preferred to ‘artificial intelligence’. Agreement (‘agree’ or ‘strongly agree’ combined) with statements relating to trust, acceptance and perceived benefit of AI was significantly higher after a structured educational session (38.2% to 67.6%, 85.3% to 97.1%, and 52.9% to 97.1% respectively; all p≤0.003). Healthcare professionals favoured an AI ‘assistant’ model over full automation, citing the need for validation, explainability, data governance and workflow integration. Patients also preferred some level of human oversight. Conclusion Patients and healthcare professionals are cautiously supportive of AI-assisted diagnosis of duodenal biopsies, conditional upon demonstration of accuracy, appropriate human oversight and transparent communication. Attitudes towards AI-assisted diagnosis were more favourable after structured explanation. Key Messages What is already known on this topic Very little is known about patients’, carers’ or healthcare professionals’ views about the automation of diagnosis in pathology, using AI-based software solutions. What this study adds ⇒ This is the first study to investigate patient, carer and healthcare professional attitudes specifically to AI-mediated duodenal biopsy diagnosis. Around two-thirds of respondents supported AI-assisted diagnosis, contingent upon clear and available evidence of accuracy, appropriate human oversight and transparent communication, together with appropriate regulatory approval of the technology. ⇒ Attitudes were markedly more favourable after a single structured educational session: agreement that AI could improve duodenal biopsy diagnosis nearly doubled and trust in healthcare AI rose substantially, suggesting that public views of AI in diagnosis can be influenced by clear explanation. ⇒ Patients and healthcare professionals both favour some ongoing level of human oversight of any AI-based diagnostic approach. How this study might affect research, practice or policy ⇒ Our study suggests that a phased, AI-assistant-first deployment model with defined validation and audit checkpoints would be most readily acceptable when introducing diagnostic AI into histopathology. ⇒ It indicates that appropriate information and education, for example, a patient and public involvement and engagement (PPIE) session, can increase trust in AI in healthcare. ⇒ It shows that patients and the public are more trusting of technology for which the term machine learning is used, rather than artificial intelligence (AI). ⇒ It offers a stakeholder-engagement template for use by others introducing AI-based diagnostics.

title: Automated segmentation of renal structures using brightfield images of unstained kidney biopsies
abstract: The automated segmentation of unstained kidney brightfield microscopy images remains a significant challenge in medical imaging. In conventional histopathology, staining provides crucial structural and molecular contrast, allowing renal compartments and structures to be readily distinguished. The absence of staining markedly reduces this contrast, obscuring the fine architectural details that are essential for diagnosis. Addressing this gap would reduce reliance on staining protocols, reduce technical and interpretive variability, and preserve valuable tissue for downstream molecular or multi-omics analyses. Ultimately, automation of unstained image segmentation could enable faster, more objective tissue analysis while preserving samples for further molecular testing. In this work, we provide a comprehensive review of state-of-the-art segmentation methods applied to renal brightfield microscopy images. Current findings highlight a predominance of Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) based architectures for semantic segmentation approaches while recent trends point to the growing application of transformer-based and instance-segmentation strategies. However, the field is still hampered by the scarcity and poor annotation of publicly available renal datasets. Aiming to further contribute to the enhancement of the field, a dataset of 18 Whole Slide Images (WSIs) of unstained human kidney tissue is made publicly available. Additionally, in the dataset, we provide 543 annotated tiles extracted from the WSIs, facilitating further research into stain-independent segmentation approaches. As a third contribution, we present a preliminary case study, evaluating state-of-the-art deep learning segmentation architectures, including U-Net and Segment Anything Model (SAM). Our preliminary results indicate that deep learning models demonstrate promising segmentation performance in unstained kidney biopsies. In alignment with these findings, advanced customised loss functions and data augmentation were integrated into the supervised training of the promising U-Net, DeepLabv3+, and TransUNet models, achieving significant improvements compared to the baseline experiments. To exploit the abundance of unlabelled data, we further tested FixMatchSeg, a semi-supervised learning method; however, its segmentation performance remained slightly behind the supervised methods. Taken together, these contributions establish a foundation for future research in stain-independent Computational Pathology, demonstrating that unstained brightfield microscopy images can reliably support downstream tissue analysis tasks. Our dataset, validation experiments, and methodological insights provide the community with both resources and benchmarks to advance robust, data-efficient, and generalisable kidney tissue segmentation.

title: Automated Gland MRI Radiomics for Predicting Time to Pathologic Progression during Prostate Cancer Active Surveillance
abstract: BackgroundRepeated biopsies burden patients during prostate cancer active surveillance (AS). Existing MRI risk stratification tools avoiding biopsy remain limited by the difficulty of automated lesion segmentation. PurposeTo develop a model integrating gland MRI radiomics and clinicopathologic variables for predicting time to pathologic progression during prostate cancer AS. Materials and MethodsThis retrospective single-institution study included men with grade group 1 or favorable grade group 2 prostate cancer undergoing AS with fusion-targeted and systematic biopsy (2010-2025). Gland segmentation used nnU-Net; gland radiomic features were selected by LASSO-penalized survival regression to train an XGBoost accelerated failure time model. Comparator models were assessed by C-index, time-dependent area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), Kaplan-Meier, and decision curve analysis. ResultsOf 522 men (median age, 64 years [IQR, 59-68]), 410 were assigned by site to development and 112 to internal testing. Gland segmentation Dice was 0.89 {+/-} 0.04. The C-index was higher for the gland radiomics model (0.77) than for clinicopathologic (0.68) and lesion radiomics (0.68) models (adjusted P [≤] .017), with the highest time-dependent AUC at 36 months (0.87 [95% CI: 0.78, 0.94]). Progression-free survival was lower in high-risk than low-risk groups (36 months, 63.9% vs 100%; 48 months, 55.4% vs 93.8%; log-rank P < .001). At a 0.25 risk threshold, 49.1% and 31.3% were low risk at 36 and 48 months (negative predictive value, 1.00; positive predictive value, 0.36). ConclusionAn automated gland radiomics model predicted time to pathologic progression during AS better than clinicopathologic and lesion-based models.

title: Virtual spatial transcriptomics links kidney histopathology to disease-associated molecular programs
abstract: Introduction Spatial transcriptomics can resolve compartment-specific molecular programs in kidney disease, but its cost and technical requirements limit its use in clinical diagnostics and in large biopsy archives. Predicting spatial gene expression from routine histology with artificial intelligence could extend molecular characterization to existing clinically annotated kidney tissue collections. Methods We adapted DeepSpot-M, a pretrained multimodal foundation model that predicts spatial gene expression from histology, using paired hematoxylin and eosin images and Visium spatial transcriptomics from 209 Kidney Precision Medicine Project (KPMP) participants. We evaluated virtual profiles in held-out human biopsies, associated them with histopathologic and biochemical injury markers in 567 rats with defined nephrotoxin exposures from a public toxicogenomics database, and generated a virtual atlas from 1 534 histology slides of 476 additional KPMP participants. Results Kidney-specific adaptation of DeepSpot-M doubled the mean Pearson correlation of each model’s 1 000 best-predicted genes (0.43 versus 0.22) and exceeded recent foundation models. Virtual profiles preserved the direction of all 13 disease-marker differences in measured expression, including tubular injury, maladaptive repair, gluconeogenesis, and fibrosis-associated programs. All 11 measured associations between molecular programs and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) were also preserved. Without rat-specific training, a virtual injury score distinguished moderate or severe histopathologic lesions (area under the curve, 0.85) and at least twofold blood urea nitrogen elevation (0.82). title: Generative Deep Learning Maps Brain Oxygen Metabolism and Its Age-Related Decline from Two Standard Noninvasive MRI Scans
abstract: PurposeTo develop a generative deep learning model mapping the cerebral metabolic rate of oxygen (CMRO2) from minimal, contrast-free MRI. Materials and MethodsThis retrospective study used 3-T MRI of healthy adults from one center (May 2015-June 2025). A conditional generative adversarial network (GAN) was trained to reproduce contrast-based analytical CMRO2 from progressively fewer quantitative MRI inputs (cerebral blood flow [CBF], T2*, T2, cerebral blood volume), T1-weighted MRI, or resting-state functional MRI. Models were trained on 54 participants and tested on 41 (25 women; mean age, 49 years {+/-} 23 [SD]), on calculation-task data, and, without retraining, on same-protocol (n = 24) and cross-vendor (n = 12) data. Agreement (r, mean absolute error [MAE]) was compared with the test-retest error of analytical CMRO2, and repeatability (n = 9) with intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs). ResultsA GAN using only CBF and T2* agreed with analytical CMRO2 as well as one adding T2 (r = 0.89 [95% CI: 0.88, 0.90] for both), with errors below the between-day test-retest error (median MAE, 38.1 vs 46.5 {micro}mol/100 g/min); CBF alone, T1-weighted MRI, and functional MRI performed worse (P [≤] .004). It was as repeatable as analytical CMRO2 (median ICC, 0.87 for both), preserved task-evoked patterns (Dice, 0.78), agreed with same-protocol (r = 0.89) and, less, cross-vendor data (r = 0.81; P [≤] .001), and captured the age-related decline (6.8 vs analytical, 5.0 {micro}mol/100 g/min per decade). ConclusionGenerative deep learning mapped brain oxygen metabolism from two contrast-free scans with repeatability comparable to the reference.

title: Distinct Relaxation Kurtosis Imaging-Derived White Matter Microstructural Phenotypes Tracking Alzheimer’s Disease Pathology and Cognitive Decline
abstract: White matter (WM) pathology is increasingly recognized as an early, mechanistically relevant feature of Alzheimer’s disease (AD), yet sensitive in-vivo biomarkers remain limited. Here, we introduce an MRI-based Relaxation Kurtosis Imaging (RKI) technique sensitive to WM microstructure. RKI metrics differentiate two distinct phenotypes of white matter that follow divergent microstructural trajectories in preclinical and early symptomatic AD. We examined their relationships to AD progression, gray matter (GM) pathology, and clinical impairment in 305 adults spanning amyloid-negative to amyloid-positive stages with normal cognition, preclinical AD, and early symptomatic AD. Pathological changes in one phenotype reflected axonal alterations without myelin loss and were anatomically coupled to GM cortical pathology, strengthening with disease stage – a signature of Wallerian degeneration. Alterations in the other phenotype represented WM demyelination. A model incorporating RKI-metrics, age, sex, amyloid status, APOE genotype, and brain volume classified Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR)-based impairment with an area under the receiver operating curve (AUC) = 0.933, with the RKI-metrics contributing 27% (second only to amyloid at 40%). While both phenotypes related comparably to concurrent cognition (each ∼27%), the “axonal” phenotype showed the strongest relationship to subsequent cognitive decline (41% of explained variance), with the “myelin” phenotype contributing 31%. These RKI-defined dual white matter phenotypes provide new insight into AD pathology, adding diagnostic and prognostic value for tracking both current cognitive status and future cognitive decline. Brief Summary A new MRI-based Relaxation Kurtosis Imaging (RKI) method characterizes two distinct white matter tissue signatures that track Alzheimer’s progression, predicting both clinical dementia stage and future cognitive decline Highlights Relaxation Kurtosis Imaging (RKI) differentiates two distinct microstructural phenotypes with different trajectories of white matter pathology in Alzheimer’s disease. The first phenotype highlights microstructural axonal alterations anatomically coupled to regional cortical pathology consistent with Wallerian neurodegeneration. The second phenotype represents demyelination diffusely connected to cortical pathology. RKI metrics track AD pathology and predict future cognitive decline.

title: Lightweight and Explainable AI for Chest Radiograph Classification in Low-Resource Settings: Cross-Dataset Generalization, Grad-CAM Verification, and Uncertainty-Aware Referral
abstract: Chest radiography is the most common imaging test worldwide, yet models trained on one hospitals data often fail elsewhere, a critical problem for low-resource hospitals that cannot collect large local datasets. This paper presents a lightweight, explainable framework for chest radiograph classification, trained and evaluated entirely on CPU with public data. EfficientNet-B0 and ResNet-18 are trained on a 10,000-image subset of NIH ChestX-ray14 and evaluated without retraining on a paediatric pneumonia set, alongside a TorchXRayVision DenseNet121 pretrained baseline and a model trained directly on paediatric data. On the NIH test set (n = 2,500), the best single model reaches pneumonia AUC-ROC 0.738 and a two-model ensemble 0.742, while an adult-trained model falls to AUC 0.454 on paediatric images, and, symmetrically, a paediatric-trained model falls to 0.473 on adult NIH images. Pooling the adult and paediatric training sets into one binary pneumonia model changes the picture: a merged EfficientNet-B0 reaches AUC 0.951 (95% CI 0.932-0.967) on paediatric images, the first result whose whole 95% CI clears 0.90, and 0.675 on NIH images with zero sensitivity at threshold 0.5, while a merged ResNet-18 reaches 0.962 on paediatric and 0.606 on NIH images. Pooling fixes the catastrophic cross-domain failure but does not recover adult-only performance, and ensembling a merged model with a single-domain model adds nothing on either test set. Grad-CAM heatmaps are shown for true positives, false negatives and false positives, and Monte Carlo dropout referral raises answered-case accuracy from 0.889 to 0.948 on NIH data but not under domain shift. All results carry bootstrap confidence intervals, and the limits of a 22-positive NIH test set are stated plainly.

title: Deep Learning Prediction of DNA Damage Response Protein Signaling from H&E Histopathology and Reverse-Phase Protein Arrays in Pan-Gynecologic and Breast Cancers
abstract: Defects in homologous recombination and the DNA damage response (DDR) make gynecologic and breast tumors sensitive to platinum chemotherapy and PARP inhibitors, but identifying them requires costly genomic testing that reads permanent genomic scars rather than current pathway activity. Routine hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) slides are available for nearly every patient. This project asked whether H&E morphology carries information about functional DDR protein signaling across five cancer types in a single model. We matched 1,673 diagnostic whole-slide images from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) to Level 4 reverse-phase protein array (RPPA) data for 1,527 patients with breast (BRCA, n = 858), endometrial (UCEC, n = 403), cervical (CESC, n = 146), ovarian (OV, n = 72), and uterine carcinosarcoma (UCS, n = 48) tumors. Slides were tiled at 0.5 μm/px and Macenko-normalized, yielding 20.4 million tiles. Tiles were embedded with two frozen pathology foundation models, UNI2-h and Virchow2. A gated attention-based multiple instance learning (ABMIL) network jointly regressed six RPPA pathway scores, including a DNA_damage composite of 11 DDR proteins. Performance was assessed by out-of-fold Spearman correlation under 5-fold, cancer-type-stratified, site-grouped cross-validation and compared against a baseline that predicts each patient's cancer-type mean. Predicted DNA_damage correlated with measured values (ρ = 0.43 for both encoders) and exceeded the cancer-type baseline (ρ = 0.31; Δ ρ = +0.13). The signal held within cancer types (within-type ρ = 0.29 for UNI2-h, 0.30 for Virchow2). With the original UNI encoder, it survived site-held-out folds with residualized targets (within-type ρ = 0.26), and it vanished when targets were shuffled within cancer type (within-type ρ ≤ 0.00 for all three encoders). All six pathway scores were predicted above baseline; Cell_cycle was strongest (ρ ≈ 0.59). In interpretability analyses, the top 10 attention tiles per slide contained more tumor (+1.8 SD), larger tumor nuclei (+1.0 to +1.3 SD), and fewer lymphocytes (-0.6 SD) than the bottom 10 tiles; 13 of 14 morphometric features differed (q < 0.05). Attention agreed with Integrated Gradients (median ρ ≈ 0.70). Routine H&E contains a moderate, reproducible signal of DDR protein abundance beyond cancer type, concentrated in tumor-dense regions with enlarged nuclei. Separating this signal from proliferation and predicting phosphorylated CHK1 and CHK2 directly are the next steps toward a functional, slide-based DDR biomarker.

title: Focused ultrasound-enhanced carboplatin delivery improves radiotherapy response and survival in a preclinical glioblastoma model
abstract: Rationale Glioblastoma is highly resistant to conventional therapies due to the limited penetration of chemotherapeutics across the blood-brain and blood-tumor barriers (BBB, BTB). Although platinum-based drugs show strong cytotoxic and radiosensitizing properties in several cancers, their inability to achieve therapeutic concentrations within the central nervous system (CNS) severely limits their efficacy in brain tumors. This study investigated whether focused ultrasound (FUS)-mediated BBB/BTB disruption combined with intravenous carboplatin and stereotactic radiotherapy could improve drug delivery, tumor control, and survival in a preclinical glioblastoma model. Methods F98 glioma-bearing rats were treated with a single dose of 15 Gy radiation therapy (RT), carboplatin only, carboplatin + RT, FUS + carboplatin or FUS + carboplatin + RT. FUS-mediated permeabilization was confirmed by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and platinum accumulation was quantified by inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry and synchrotron X-ray fluorescence. Tumor progression and microenvironmental changes were monitored using multiparametric MRI (diffusion, perfusion, and vascular permeability), followed by voxel-wise clustering analysis and histopathological validation. Results The FUS + carboplatin + RT group demonstrated the strongest therapeutic benefit, compared to all other treatment groups, yielding up to a 122% increase in median survival relative to the untreated group. This treatment also reduced necrotic core expansion and induced a transient increase in tumor perfusion, suggesting improved vascular function. FUS enhanced carboplatin delivery to both the tumor and peritumoral brain, with platinum distribution closely correlating with MRI signal enhancement. Voxel-wise clustering of multiparametric MRI identified biologically distinct tumor regions that were subsequently validated by immunohistochemistry. Conclusion The combination of FUS-mediated carboplatin delivery and radiotherapy represents a safe, non-invasive strategy that enhances drug delivery and improves survival in an aggressive preclinical model of glioblastoma. By overcoming a major limitation of current therapies, this approach shows promising potential for clinical translation.

title: A Deep Operator Network to Predict Thermal Dose on Brain Tumors in MRI-Guided Laser Induced Thermal Therapy: with Synthetic Data
abstract: Background MRI-guided laser interstitial thermal therapy (LITT) provides minimally invasive option for surgical treatment of recurrent brain tumors. While patient-specific prediction of thermal dose distributions would improve treatment planning, no quantitative methods currently exist for this purpose. Although conventional numerical solvers are being widely investigated, these methods are computationally expensive and often limited by accuracy and reliability. Purpose Here we propose DeepoLITT, a rapid and accurate model to predict quantitatively heat propagation in LITT procedures. This study represents the first phase of the investigation which focuses on training and validating synthetic datasets to test model’s accuracy, robustness, and computational efficiency. Methods We built DeepoLITT on a branch–trunk neural network architecture, where the first branch extracts feature from tumor images, the second branch encodes laser parameters (power, duration, and probe orientation), and the trunk models the mapping from spatial coordinates to the resulting temperature field. To train and test the model, we generated synthetic datasets with different noise levels (0∼20%) to mimic LITT procedures with two distinct laser probe types (FullFire and SideFire [Monteris, Inc.]) by a FEM (finite element method) solver. The dataset consisted of 400 samples, of which 90% were used for training and validation and 10% for testing. To evaluate spatial similarity of predicted thermal dose distribution against the ground truth, we employed Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) and Hausdorff Distance (HD) computed on CEM43 (Cumulative Equivalent Minutes at 43 °C) isodose contours at thresholds of 2, 10, and 60 minutes. Finally, we evaluated the model’s inference speed with a representative image grid. Results For the FullFire laser probe, the DeepoLITT model achieved temperature prediction error with average values ranging from 1.16±0.40% to 2.92±0.25%, and peak values ranging from 4.26±1.31% to 14.94±0.43% as data noise increased from 0% to 20%. For the SideFire laser probe, the model achieved temperature prediction error with average values ranging from 3.79±0.53% to 5.13±1.00% and peak values ranging from 15.18±7.15% to 20.75±2.84%. For thermal dose assessment, at the noise-free level for the FullFire laser probe, the model exhibited strong spatial agreement with FEM references, yielding DSCs of 0.96±0.02, 0.97±0.21, and 0.96±0.21 with corresponding HDs of 0.09±0.08 mm, 0.07±0.07 mm, and 0.06±0.08 mm at 2-, 10-, and 60-minute CEM43 thresholds. For the SideFire laser probe, the model achieved DSCs of 0.96±0.02, 0.97±0.21, and 0.96±0.21, with corresponding HDs of 0.20±0.31mm, 0.11±0.30 mm, and 0.15±0.31 mm, respectively. As the noise level increases, these DSC values show a decreasing trend, and the HD values increase. In terms of computational efficiency, the DeepoLITT model inferences temperature maps with 0.04±0.05 seconds per 3D sample ([31 × 31 × 3] grid), compared to 24.32±2.12 seconds required by the FEM solver. Conclusions The study with synthetic data demonstrates the proposed model is an accurate and rapid method in predicting thermal dose. After testing clinical data, the method has high feasibility to be deployed in real clinical environment.

title: Sc-HistoMorphomics: A General Framework for High-throughput, Multimodal Profiling of Nuclear Morphology in Tissues
abstract: Quantitative cellular morphology provides a rich but underutilized window into cell identity and state. We introduce sc-HistoMorphomics, a scalable framework for profiling nuclear morphology in whole-slide H&E images and correlating these measurements with spatial transcriptomics data. Our pipeline combines deep-learning based segmentation with 194 interpretable morphometric features capturing nuclear shape, eosin and hematoxylin texture, and neighbourhood architecture, enabling high-throughput, multimodal characterization of tissue organization. Applied to endometrium, breast cancer tissue, and pancreas, sc-HistoMorphomics revealed conserved high-dimensional feature structure across tissues and reproducible association between morphology and gene expression. Eosin-based texture features were associated with senescence signatures in endometrium, and morphology-based clustering recapitulated broad stromal, lymphocyte, and epithelial tumor cell classes in breast cancer. In pancreas, negative correlations between CDKN1A and multiple morphological features were consistent across cell types and donors. Together, these results establish sc-HistoMorphomics as a generalizable and interpretable tool for linking morphology with spatially resolved molecular state across diverse tissues.

title: Fine-tuned encoders, generative large language models and typed decisions for classifying findings in chest CT reports: paired English-Japanese internal testing and external testing on naturally written Japanese reports
abstract: PurposeTo compare fine-tuned encoders, generative large language models (LLMs) and typed decisions (per-finding yes/no questions answered with a probability) for classifying 18 findings in chest CT reports, and to identify when typed decisions help. MethodsThis retrospective study used public data. The internal test set comprised 150 CT-RATE reports with paired Japanese translations at three quality levels; the external test set, 243 naturally written Japanese reports with human annotations (RR-Findings). title: Circulating miRNA profiling identifies hsa-miR-23a-3p and a three-miRNA signature associated with serous ovarian cancer
abstract: High-grade serous ovarian carcinoma (HGSOC) is the most lethal subtype of epithelial ovarian cancer, highlighting the need for minimally invasive biomarkers that support disease detection and molecular characterization. Circulating microRNAs (miRNAs) have emerged as promising candidates, although their clinical applicability remains limited by methodological variability and insufficient validation. Plasma samples from 100 individuals (50 patients with ovarian cancer and 50 cancer-free controls) were initially collected from four biobanks. Following quality control, 94 samples (47 patients and 47 controls) were included in the final analysis. Eight candidate miRNAs were quantified using RT-qPCR, and relative expression was assessed following global mean normalization. Differential expression was evaluated using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test, while discriminatory performance was assessed using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis. Three-miRNA logistic regression models were additionally explored using repeated stratified five-fold cross-validation. Among the eight candidates, hsa-miR-23a-3p exhibited significantly lower circulating expression in patients with ovarian cancer than in controls (p = 2.14 × 10 −5 ), achieving an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.755 (95% CI, 0.657-0.852), with 93.6% sensitivity and 53.2% specificity at the selected threshold. Exploratory analysis across FIGO stages revealed heterogeneous expression patterns, although the limited number of early-stage cases precluded definitive conclusions regarding stage-specific performance. A three-miRNA signature comprising hsa-miR-23a-3p, hsa-miR-21-5p, and hsa-miR-20a-5p achieved an apparent AUC of 0.798. However, repeated cross-validation yielded a mean AUC of 0.716 ± 0.022, indicating reduced performance after internal validation. Variability in exogenous spike-in Ct values and the marked imbalance in biobank representation between study groups highlighted potential pre-analytical confounding. Circulating hsa-miR-23a-3p showed moderate discriminatory performance between patients with ovarian cancer and cancer-free controls, supporting its further investigation as a candidate liquid biopsy biomarker. Although combining three miRNAs improved apparent classification performance, this advantage was not established through internal validation. These findings underscore the importance of accounting for sample provenance, technical variability, and model overfitting when evaluating circulating miRNA signatures. Independent validation in appropriately balanced cohorts is required before clinical applicability can be established.

title: Pyrenophora teres f. teres uses specialized infection structures to facilitate effector-driven promotion of in planta colonization on barley
abstract: Pyrenophora teres f. teres is a necrotrophic fungal pathogen that causes net form net blotch (NFNB) of barley. Infection of susceptible barley leaves initially causes dot-like lesions that progress to transverse and longitudinal striations, that form the net-like pattern of necrosis for which the disease was named. While the complex genetic architecture of the P. teres f. teres -barley interaction involves both dominant resistance and susceptibility and quantitative resistance, the in planta infection structures, compatible infection timeline, and the influence of effectors remain poorly defined. This study used fluorescent staining and confocal laser scanning microscopy (CLSM) to define infection structures and characterize the compatible infection timeline of P. teres f. teres . Using CLSM in conjunction with image-segmentation machine learning, we generated a clear comparative infection timeline showing how P. teres f. teres isolates harboring zero, one, or two virulence effector alleles infect the barley cultivar Rika. We believe that the effector genes VR1 and VR2 contributed to virulence in a synergistic manner. The effector genes’ combined presence accelerated the timing and spread of programmed cell death, resulting in significantly greater hyphal volume and visibly more severe macroscopic lesion development. This suggests that P. teres f. teres uses specialized infection structures alongside effectors to maximize fungal colonization and hyphal positioning to optimize nutrient uptake, perpetuating its polycyclic life cycle.

title: Automated aortoiliac calcification segmentation from arterial-phase computed tomography scans: development and validation
abstract: IntroductionArterial calcium is widely used as a biomarker for coronary artery disease but is underutilized in peripheral artery disease (PAD) due to challenges in automated measurement of peripheral vascular calcium. We developed a fully automated deep-learning pipeline for measurement of aortoiliac calcium from arterial-phase, contrast-enhanced abdominopelvic computed tomography angiography (CTA) to extract this important PAD biomarker. MethodsThe pipeline uses two nnU-Net models for aortoiliac arterial segmentation and identification of calcified voxels. We trained on 56 computed tomography (CT) scans and validated on 106 scans by comparing the pipelines calcium estimation from CTA against calcium burden on corresponding non-contrast phase CT within manually segmented arterial contours across a range of radiodensity thresholds (100-1000 Hounsfield units [HU]). Using the non-contrast HU threshold that maximized correlation between measures, we performed linear regression with five-fold cross-validation between pipeline-estimated and non-contrast calcium quantities, and risk reclassification analysis across quartiles using Monte Carlo simulations to compare pipeline and non-contrast-derived calcium burden quartiles while measuring quadratically weighted kappa. ResultsNon-contrast calcium burden calculated from voxels with attenuation [≥]400 HU correlated best with CTA calcium burden (Pearson r=0.952 for aortic calcium; Pearson r=0.955 for iliofemoral calcium) and was used for subsequent analysis. Five-fold cross-validation of non-contrast calcium volume prediction from pipeline-estimated CTA calcium burden, using [≥]400 HU to define non-contrast calcium voxels, demonstrated aggregated Pearson r>0.91 for all held-out folds in all three arterial regions tested. In risk reclassification analysis, quadratically weighted kappa for agreement between predicted and ground truth calcium quartile classifications was {kappa}=0.88 for the aorta, {kappa}=0.84 for bilateral iliofemoral arteries, and {kappa}=0.80 for all regions. ConclusionAortoiliac calcium burden can be accurately quantified from CTA with excellent reproducibility against calcium voxels [≥]400 HU on non-contrast imaging. Quantification of this important biomarker expands opportunities for improved peripheral vascular disease diagnosis and risk prediction. title: NeuroImgAgent: a multi-agent platform for cross-species fMRI analysis with evidence-gated quality control
abstract: Cross-species functional MRI analysis requires coordinating specialized workflows and assessing intermediate outputs. We present NeuroImgAgent, a multi-agent platform driven by large language models that translates natural-language requests into workflows for humans, macaques, rats and mice. Quantitative checks and vision-language model assessments determine whether processing continues, enters bounded recovery or stops. Across 268 paired cases, preprocessing metrics were broadly comparable to those of fMRIPrep, AFNI and RABIES. With GPT-5.5, NeuroImgAgent corrected 111 of 120 induced orientation errors and passed all 52 intent-recognition and planning tasks, 8 of 9 recovery tasks and 11 of 14 tool-construction tasks on NeuroAgentBench. In 120 paired challenge cases, the full configuration increased usability from 76.7% to 92.5%, as assessed by blinded experts, and reduced unusable outputs delivered without warning from 18.3% to 4.2% of cases relative to quality-control ablation.

title: Retinal Vessel Volume Density and Intraoperative Cortical Vascular Phenotypes in Moyamoya Disease
abstract: Background Angiographic staging describes large-artery stenosis and collateral evolution in moyamoya disease but does not directly depict the cortical surface vasculature, which can vary among patients with similar Suzuki stages. We examined whether a side-matched three-dimensional retinal vascular measure was associated with intraoperative cortical vascular phenotypes after accounting for Suzuki stage. Methods This prospective single-center cohort included 52 patients with moyamoya disease who underwent combined direct and indirect revascularization; 48 had analyzable retinal vessel volume density (RVVD) in the side-matched eye. RVVD was defined as the percentage of the corresponding retinal tissue volume occupied by three-dimensional optical coherence tomography angiography vascular signal within the central 6 × 6-mm region from the retinal nerve fiber layer to the inner plexiform layer. After dural opening and before vascular manipulation, overall cortical vascular richness and arterial, venous, and small-vessel richness were graded from 0 to 3. Associations were evaluated with Spearman correlation and proportional-odds ordinal logistic regression adjusted for age, sex, and ipsilateral Suzuki stage. Results Mean RVVD was 12.92% (SD, 3.30 percentage points). Higher RVVD was associated with greater overall cortical vascular richness (ρ=0.523; bias-corrected and accelerated bootstrap 95% CI, 0.279-0.714; P<0.001) and arterial richness (ρ=0.522; 95% CI, 0.261-0.714; P<0.001). Per 1-SD higher RVVD, the adjusted cumulative odds ratio for being in a higher richness category was 3.92 (95% CI, 1.82-8.44; P<0.001) for overall cortical vascular richness and 4.31 (95% CI, 1.92-9.70; P<0.001) for arterial richness. Conclusions In moyamoya disease, higher side-matched RVVD was associated with richer overall and arterial cortical vascular phenotypes at revascularization surgery, independent of Suzuki stage. Three-dimensional retinal vascular imaging may therefore provide a noninvasive, side-specific preoperative measure of cortical vascular remodeling. title: Within-scan MRI signal and texture in Alzheimer disease: a multicohort study
abstract: INTRODUCTIONConventional MRI contains tissue signal and texture information beyond regional volume, but acquisition variability limits their comparability. We evaluated within-scan signal and texture analyses for estimating contemporaneous cognition and amyloid/tau burden in Alzheimers disease (AD) beyond volumetry. METHODSWe retrospectively analyzed 2,437 baseline datasets from ADNI3, ADNI4, MCSA, SCAN/CLARiTI, and OASIS-3. SynthSeg defined regions for T1-weighted and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) measurements. Within-scan regional-to-rest log ratios (WSRLR) were compared with scanner-matched, cross-fitted cognitively normal (CN) references. Texture analysis used three-dimensional gray-level co-occurrence matrices (GLCM). Covariate-adjusted rank models examined associations; ADNI3-trained ridge, elastic-net, gradient-boosting, and TabPFN-v2 models were tested externally. RESULTSModerate-to-strong correlations were observed between regional signal changes assessed using WSRLR vs. CN-reference (cohort median regional {rho}=0.504-0.890; n=2,314). Lower entorhinal FLAIR WSRLR and greater entropy were associated with AD dementia adjusted for volume, while opposite correlations were observed with the hippocampus (all q<0.001). Greater entorhinal FLAIR entropy correlated with lower Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) and Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) scores (r=-0.198 and -0.098, respectively; both q<0.001). Lower entorhinal FLAIR WSRLR and T1 cluster shade were associated with higher regional tau uptake beyond volume and diagnosis (r=-0.146 and -0.205; both q[≤]0.010). Adding entorhinal and hippocampal signal and texture significantly improved pooled external MoCA (n=868) and MMSE (n=551) prediction in three of four models. DISCUSSIONWithin-scan signal and texture demonstrated AD-related regional associations and improved prediction of contemporaneous cognitive performance beyond volumetry. Prospective validation is needed to evaluate their potential value in opportunistic dementia screening.

title: Adapting Echocardiographic Foundation Models for Detecting Pulmonary Embolism-Related Right-Heart Strain
abstract: Pulmonary embolism (PE) is a time-sensitive medical emergency in which rapid recognition of right ventricular (RV) dysfunction by point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) can support early risk stratification. Here, we present HOPE (ecHO-Pulmonary Embolism), a real-world emergency cardiac POCUS video dataset comprising 4,069 patients with suspected PE, and EchoPE1, a foundation-model-based video classification framework for detecting PE-associated right-heart phenotypes. HOPE includes five commonly acquired emergency echocardiographic views, with all positive PE cases confirmed by computed tomography pulmonary angiography. EchoPE builds on EchoPrime-pretrained echocardiographic representations and incorporates view recognition, task-specific adaptation, and attention-based interpretability. Experiments suggested that directly transferring EchoPrime representations to this disease-specific task provided limited performance, whereas EchoPE (AUROC 95.2 {+/-} .3) substantially outperformed both EchoPrime with a classification head (AUROC 87.6 {+/-} 1) and conventional video deep learning baselines. At a fixed sensitivity of 90%, EchoPE achieved a precision of 87.8, compared with 70.7 for EchoPrime. Among adaptation strategies, Low-Rank Adaptation combined with knowledge distillation provided the best balance between PE discrimination and preservation of pretrained echocardiographic semantics. Interpretability analyses showed that the adapted model focused on clinically relevant RV morphological changes, interventricular septal configuration, and informative temporal segments within ultrasound videos. Overall, HOPE and EchoPE demonstrate that echocardiographic foundation models require dataset-specific adaptation to identify PE-related right-heart strain and support the potential use of artificial intelligence-assisted bedside echocardiography for risk warning in acute care settings.

title: EpiCycle: A flexible approach for scalable, three-dimensional reconstructions of complex epithelial tissues
abstract: Understanding organ development and repair requires methods to precisely describe cell geometry. Recent image analysis methods allow increasingly accurate segmentation of simple epithelial tissues. However, many vertebrate organs contain more complex stratified epithelia, for which accurate 3D cellular segmentation remains challenging. Here, we describe EpiCycle, an iterative, user-friendly approach developed to address the unique segmentation challenges posed by stratified epithelia. Starting from sparse or no ground truth annotations, EpiCycle guides users through a human-in-the-loop refinement process that culminates in 3D consensus reconstruction. Through cyclical correction, annotation and model retraining, EpiCycle allows users to progressively build robust, dataset-specific segmentation models while simultaneously generating 3D ground truth. To highlight the utility of EpiCycle, we train models that generate high-confidence, tissue-level segmentation of the stratified squamous epithelium in adult zebrafish skin. We apply our approach to segmentation of mouse embryonic branching salivary glands demonstrating its versatility across organs and species. Finally, we produce and analyze quantitative measurements of stratified cell geometry in human fetal epidermis. Thus, EpiCycle enables scalable and quantitative 3D reconstructions of complex vertebrate tissues without relying on pre-existing ground truth.

title: Being Born versus Being Born Early: Disentangling Birth from Prematurity in Perinatal Brain Development
abstract: ABSTRACT Studies of preterm birth report both delayed and accelerated brain maturation, depending on whether preterm infants are compared with term newborns or with fetuses. We propose that these mixed observations arise because such comparisons conflate two distinct influences, the effect of birth on term-aged infants and the independent effects of being born prematurely. Using MRI data from 330 term and 118 preterm neonates in the developing Human Connectome Project (dHCP), we developed a simple piecewise linear model that estimates prenatal and postnatal rates of development separately for term and preterm infants across volumetric, microstructural and connectivity measures. In term infants, birth accelerated volumetric growth, with total brain volume growing 44% faster post-birth, with regionally specific alterations in microstructural trajectories. Deep white matter continued to mature, whereas superficial and cerebellar white matter reversed direction. Changes in cortical connectivity at birth followed the sensorimotor to association axis, shifting towards specialisation in sensory and insular cortex and towards more diverse connectivity in association cortex. In contrast, the effect of birth on preterm infants was much weaker, where development largely continued at prenatal rates. These results show that the impact of birth depends on brain region and maturational state at birth. Separating birth from prematurity offers a framework for interpreting mixed findings in the perinatal literature.

Studies of preterm birth report both delayed and accelerated brain maturation, depending on whether preterm infants are compared with term newborns or with fetuses. We propose that these mixed observations arise because such comparisons conflate two distinct influences, the effect of birth on term-aged infants and the independent effects of being born prematurely. Using MRI data from 330 term and 118 preterm neonates in the developing Human Connectome Project (dHCP), we developed a simple piecewise linear model that estimates prenatal and postnatal rates of development separately for term and preterm infants across volumetric, microstructural and connectivity measures. In term infants, birth accelerated volumetric growth, with total brain volume growing 44% faster post-birth, with regionally specific alterations in microstructural trajectories. Deep white matter continued to mature, whereas superficial and cerebellar white matter reversed direction. Changes in cortical connectivity at birth followed the sensorimotor to association axis, shifting towards specialisation in sensory and insular cortex and towards more diverse connectivity in association cortex. In contrast, the effect of birth on preterm infants was much weaker, where development largely continued at prenatal rates. These results show that the impact of birth depends on brain region and maturational state at birth. Separating birth from prematurity offers a framework for interpreting mixed findings in the perinatal literature.

title: Confidence-Aware Adaptation for Medical Image Segmentation Under Acquisition Shift
abstract: Medical image segmentation models can lose accuracy and produce unreliable confidence estimates when deployed across acquisition centres. We study StaRFM, an adaptation objective that combines a Fisher information penalty (FIP) with a confidence misalignment penalty (CMP), and examine how the spatial aggregation of CMP affects lesion segmentation. We evaluate a Segment Anything Model (SAM) adaptation on five MRI and CT datasets and conduct a controlled leave-centre-out experiment on ISLES~2022 using a 3D U-Net. The SAM experiments improve mean Dice by 2.3 percentage points relative to fine-tuned SAM; calibration was not measured for those models. In the ISLES experiment, the baseline achieved 73.0\% Dice, 7.71\% boundary expected calibration error (bECE), and $1.03\times10^{-2}$ negative log-likelihood (NLL) on 52 held-out-centre cases. A class-balanced CMP variant achieved 74.8\% Dice, 6.57\% bECE, and $0.59\times10^{-2}$ NLL; a boundary-restricted variant achieved 74.1\% Dice, 6.24\% bECE, and $0.58\times10^{-2}$ NLL. In contrast, stronger voxel-averaged CMP reduced Dice, and FIP offered no measurable additional benefit in this controlled study. Because the balanced and boundary variants were developed after an initial negative experiment, these results are exploratory. Complementary vision-language experiments and mathematical analysis characterise the broader objective, without establishing clinical reliability or a general calibration guarantee under shift. Our findings highlight the importance of class imbalance and boundary-aware evaluation when designing confidence penalties for medical segmentation.
